title: Depression in adults
blurb: Classify depression as less or more severe, match first-line options to the person's choice with NICE NG222, and know when psychotic depression or ECT applies.
question: Rachel, 34, has a PHQ-9 score of 11 after a relationship breakdown. She is sleeping poorly, has no suicidal thoughts and would rather not take tablets. Which first-line approach best fits NICE NG222?

teach.body: NICE NG222 groups a new episode of depression into two bands. Less severe covers subthreshold and mild depression; more severe covers moderate and severe depression. As a guide, a PHQ-9 score under 16 indicates less severe and 16 or more indicates more severe. In plain English: the band guides which treatments to discuss first, but the person's own choice, after information on benefits and harms, decides between them.

rows.label: Others
values: Group CBT or BA, individual CBT or BA, exercise, mindfulness, IPT, SSRI, counselling, STPP
Individual CBT, BA, antidepressant, problem-solving, counselling, STPP, IPT, guided self-help, group exercise

rows.label: First line?
values: All can be; least intrusive first

teach.caption: NG222 1.5.2-1.5.3 and 1.6.1. Options are listed in NICE's order of effectiveness and cost; the person chooses with the clinician.

teach.body: CBT looks at how thoughts, beliefs, feelings and behaviour interact and teaches coping skills; it is structured, goal-oriented and uses homework. Behavioural activation (BA) focuses on the link between activities and mood: it helps the person spot patterns of avoidance and plan practical changes towards activities linked with better mood. BA suits people whose depression has led to withdrawal and inactivity. For more severe depression, individual CBT is usually 16 sessions.

teach.caption: Stepped or matched care delivers the least intrusive effective treatment first and steps up if needed (NG222 1.16.1 and terms).

teach.body: NICE says consider ECT for severe depression if the person chooses it based on past experience, if a rapid response is needed (for example life-threatening depression where the person is not eating or drinking), or if other treatments have failed. The person must be fully informed of risks, including anaesthetic risks and cognitive impairment. If they cannot consent, ECT is given only if it does not conflict with a valid advance decision, and MHA s58A safeguards apply to detained patients.

With a PHQ-9 of 11, Rachel has less severe depression. Her practice nurse, Nurse Lee, asks directly about suicidal thoughts (none), explains the NG222 options and starts with the least intrusive: guided self-help based on CBT or behavioural activation, through NHS Talking Therapies. She does not push antidepressants, which NICE says are not routine first line for less severe depression unless the person prefers them, and arranges a review.

teach.text: Combined CBT and an antidepressant is the first-listed option for more severe depression, but it is NOT the only first-line option: NICE says every treatment in table 2 can be first line, chosen with the person. And for less severe depression, antidepressants are not routine first line unless the person prefers them.

items: Less severe = subthreshold or mild (PHQ-9 under 16); more severe = moderate or severe (16+).
Less severe: all table 1 options can be first line; consider guided self-help first; no routine antidepressants.
More severe: all table 2 options can be first line, combined CBT plus antidepressant listed first.
Always ask about suicidal ideation; urgent referral if considerable immediate risk.
Psychotic depression: specialist care, consider antipsychotic plus antidepressant; ECT for severe, life-threatening or resistant cases.

summary: You can now classify a depressive episode as less or more severe and discuss the full range of NICE NG222 first-line options with the person. You know how psychotic depression is managed and when ECT is considered.

A.q: Under NICE NG222, which PHQ-9 score is used as the guide for 'more severe' depression?
A.why: NG222 terms: a PHQ-9 score of 16 or more was used to define more severe depression; under 16 is less severe.

whyNot.0: A score of 10 to 15 falls in the less severe band in NG222.
whyNot.3: A score of 5 would be less severe.

A.q: For less severe depression, which treatment does NICE suggest considering first because it is least intrusive?
A.why: NG222 1.5.2: all table 1 treatments can be first line, but consider the least intrusive and least resource-intensive first: guided self-help.

whyNot.0: NG222 1.5.3: do not routinely offer antidepressants first line for less severe depression.
whyNot.1: STPP is an option but not the least intrusive.
whyNot.2: IPT is an option but not the least intrusive.

A.q: Which statement about first-line treatment for more severe depression is correct under NG222?
options: Combined CBT and an antidepressant is the sole first-line option
Antidepressants should be tried before any therapy
Any treatment in table 2 can be first line
Guided self-help must be tried before other options
A.why: NG222 1.6.1: all treatments in table 2 can be used as first-line treatments; combined CBT and an antidepressant is listed first, but the choice is shared.

whyNot.0: It is listed first but NICE says all table 2 options can be first line.
whyNot.1: NICE does not require medication before therapy.
whyNot.3: There is no requirement to try guided self-help first in more severe depression.

B.q: Gwen, 47, has a PHQ-9 of 19 and low energy, and has stopped seeing friends. She prefers talking therapy to medication. What is the best response?
options: Explain that she must take an antidepressant first
Advise group exercise and review in 6 months
Wait to see if her mood improves on its own
Offer an individual therapy such as CBT or BA
B.why: PHQ-9 19 is more severe. NG222 1.6.1: all table 2 options can be first line, including individual CBT and behavioural activation; her preference guides the choice.

whyNot.0: Medication is one option, not a requirement.
whyNot.1: Group exercise is an option, but a 6-month review is too long for more severe depression.
whyNot.2: Watchful waiting is not appropriate for more severe depression.

B.q: Omar, 58, with less severe depression, says he does not want any treatment now. What does NG222 recommend?
options: Prescribe an SSRI in case he changes his mind
Refer him to the community mental health team
B.why: NG222 1.5.1: discuss concerns, give information, make sure he knows he can change his mind and arrange a further assessment, normally within 2 to 4 weeks.

whyNot.1: Prescribing against his wishes is not appropriate.
whyNot.3: Specialist referral is not indicated for less severe depression without risk.

B.q: Lily, 40, has depression and becomes withdrawn and inactive. Which therapy focuses on the link between her activities and her mood?
B.why: NG222 tables: BA focuses on the link between activities and mood, helping people reduce avoidance and plan activities linked with better mood.

whyNot.1: Psychodynamic therapy explores underlying conflicts, not activity scheduling.
whyNot.2: Family intervention is a psychosis treatment.

C.q: Arthur, 72, has severe depression. He has stopped eating and drinking for 4 days and is becoming dehydrated. He has capacity and agrees to treatment. Which treatment does NICE suggest considering because a rapid response is needed?
C.why: NG222 1.13.1: consider ECT for severe depression if a rapid response is needed, for example when depression is life-threatening because the person is not eating or drinking.

whyNot.0: Guided self-help is for less severe depression and is not rapid.
whyNot.2: Group BA will not act quickly enough in a life-threatening state.
whyNot.3: IPT will not act quickly enough in a life-threatening state.

C.q: Joan, 55, has severe depression and believes her insides are rotting and she is being punished. What does NICE NG222 advise?
options: Refer to specialists; consider an antipsychotic
Treat with an antidepressant alone in primary care
Offer guided self-help and review her in 2 weeks
Start an antipsychotic without an antidepressant
C.why: These are nihilistic delusions: psychotic depression. NG222 1.12.1-1.12.2: refer to specialist mental health services and consider an antidepressant combined with an antipsychotic.

whyNot.2: Guided self-help is not appropriate for psychotic depression.
whyNot.3: NICE suggests combining with an antidepressant, not an antipsychotic alone.

C.q: Hamid, 30, has more severe depression. At review he says he has a plan to end his life this week and has stockpiled tablets. What should the nurse do?
options: Note it and review at his next routine appointment
Ask him to complete a risk scale and then score it
Refer him urgently to specialist services
Start guided self-help to improve his coping first
C.why: NG222 1.2.8-1.2.9: always ask directly about suicidal ideation and intent; if there is considerable immediate risk, refer urgently to specialist mental health services. Means restriction is also needed.

whyNot.0: A plan and means mean immediate risk; routine review is unsafe.
whyNot.1: NICE NG225 warns against using risk scales to decide care.
whyNot.3: Self-help does not respond to immediate suicide risk.

reteach.title: Band first, choice second
reteach.question: How do you match depression treatment to the person?

blocks.body: Step 1: decide the band (less severe under PHQ-9 16; more severe 16 or more) and check risk. Step 2: share the menu. Less severe: start least intrusive, usually guided self-help; no routine antidepressants. More severe: any table 2 option can be first line, combined CBT and antidepressant listed first.

blocks.text: Combined CBT and an antidepressant is listed first, not the only first-line choice.

explain.body: Less severe: subthreshold and mild (PHQ-9 under 16). More severe: moderate and severe (PHQ-9 16 or more). The band guides the treatment discussion.

test.q: Which depressions does NG222 group as 'less severe'?
test.why: NG222: less severe depression encompasses subthreshold and mild depression.

whyNot.0: These form the more severe band.
whyNot.1: Moderate depression is in the more severe band.

explain.body: Do not routinely offer antidepressants as first-line treatment for less severe depression; offer them if that is the person's informed preference.

test.q: Sue, 29, has mild depression and, after discussion, prefers to take an antidepressant. What does NICE say?
options: Offer it, as it is her informed choice
Refuse, as talking therapy must come first
Offer it after 6 months of guided self-help
Refer her to a consultant psychiatrist first
test.why: NG222 1.5.3: do not routinely offer antidepressants first line for less severe depression, unless that is the person's informed preference.

whyNot.2: No fixed period of self-help is required.
whyNot.3: Psychiatric referral is not needed for mild depression.

explain.body: Refer to specialist services for coordinated care, risk and needs assessment. Consider an antidepressant with an antipsychotic (for example olanzapine or quetiapine). Psychological therapy after acute psychotic symptoms improve.

test.q: Which antipsychotics does NG222 give as examples for psychotic depression?
test.why: NG222 1.12.2: consider combining an antidepressant with an antipsychotic, for example olanzapine or quetiapine.

whyNot.0: Clozapine is for treatment-resistant schizophrenia, not NG222's example.
whyNot.1: These are not the examples NG222 gives.
whyNot.3: These are not the examples NG222 gives.

explain.body: Consider for severe depression if chosen from past experience, if a rapid response is needed, or if other treatments failed. Inform about anaesthetic and cognitive risks. Without capacity: only if no conflict with a valid advance decision.

test.q: Which adverse effect of ECT does NICE highlight in particular when informing people?
test.why: NG222 1.13.2: inform people of the risks, including general anaesthetic risks and potential adverse events, in particular cognitive impairment.

whyNot.0: Weight gain is a medication side effect, not the ECT risk NICE names.
whyNot.1: Hair loss is not an ECT risk named by NICE.
